title: January 6th 'Fight Like Hell' - Inciting Insurrection
description_medium: On January 6, 2021, Donald Trump addressed supporters as Congress met to count electoral votes, repeating false claims about the 2020 result and urging the crowd to “fight like hell.” A mob breached the Capitol and interrupted the count. Later that day, Trump asked the crowd to leave while saying, “we love you; you’re very special.”
description_long: On January 6, 2021, Donald Trump delivered a speech to thousands of supporters gathered in Washington D.C., repeatedly claiming the 2020 election was 'stolen' and urging them to march to the Capitol to 'fight like hell' or 'you're not going to have a country anymore.' Trump told the crowd 'we're going to walk down to the Capitol' and 'if you don't fight like hell, you're not going to have a country anymore,' while promoting false claims about election fraud that had been rejected by courts, election officials, and his own administration. Following his speech, thousands of Trump supporters stormed the U.S. Capitol, breaking windows, assaulting police officers, and forcing lawmakers to flee for their lives as they attempted to certify Joe Biden's electoral victory. Five people died during the attack, including Capitol Police officer Brian Sicknick, and more than 140 police officers were injured. Trump initially resisted calls to tell his supporters to leave, instead tweeting criticism of Vice President Mike Pence while the Capitol was under siege. When he finally released a video hours later, he told the rioters 'we love you, you're very special' while asking them to go home. The January 6th attack represented the culmination of Trump's months-long campaign to overturn the election results and marked the first time a sitting president incited an attack on the U.S. Capitol. Trump was impeached for 'incitement of insurrection' but acquitted by Senate Republicans.

title: Signs Asylum Cooperative Agreement with Honduras
description_short: The U.S. signed an Asylum Cooperative Agreement with Honduras, redirecting asylum seekers to apply there.
description_medium: The United States signed an Asylum Cooperative Agreement with Honduras in 2019, creating a route for some asylum seekers arriving at the U.S. border to seek protection in Honduras. The supplied record does not identify who could be transferred, the agreement’s implementation date or what protections were available there.

title: Pardons Rick Renzi
description_short: Trump pardoned former Rep. Rick Renzi, who had been convicted on corruption charges.
description_medium: Former U.S. Rep. Rick Renzi, an Arizona Republican, was among the people President Donald Trump pardoned. Renzi had been convicted in a federal corruption case, and Trump’s pardon addressed that conviction. The supplied account gives no offense details, grant date or stated reason for clemency.

title: Pardons Paul L. Behrens
description_short: Trump granted a presidential pardon to Paul L. Behrens as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: The Justice Department’s Jan. 13, 2021 clemency list records President Donald Trump’s pardon of Paul L. Behrens. It lists two counts of health-care fraud, two counts of false statements related to health-care matters, a 24-month prison sentence and two years of supervised release. The table gives no case narrative or pardon rationale.

preserved_fields.title: Pardons Paul L. Behrens
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump granted a presidential pardon to Paul L. Behrens as part of a clemency list.

notes: The supplied Justice Department Office of the Pardon Attorney page loaded (HTTP 200) as “Pardons Granted by President Donald J. Trump (2017-2021).” Under the January 13, 2021 section, it lists Paul L. Behrens in the Middle District of Florida, with a May 19, 2014 sentence of 24 months’ imprisonment and two years’ supervised release for two counts each of making false statements related to health-care matters and health-care fraud.

The official table confirms the listed offenses and sentence but supplies no underlying scheme narrative, affected parties, pardon rationale, or consequences. Those case-specific materials remain necessary for the requested fuller account; inferring them from the offense labels would exceed the source.

title: Commutes Sentence of Mark Shapiro
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Mark Shapiro as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: The Justice Department’s commutations list records President Donald Trump’s reduction of Mark Shapiro’s sentence in a Southern District of New York fraud case. It lists 1,020 months in prison, three years of supervised release and more than $22 million in restitution for securities, wire and mail fraud offenses. The table does not describe the scheme or the reason for commutation.

preserved_fields.title: Commutes Sentence of Mark Shapiro
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Mark Shapiro as part of a clemency list.

notes: The supplied Justice Department Office of the Pardon Attorney page loaded (HTTP 200) as “Commutations granted by President Donald J. Trump (2017-2021).” In the December 23, 2020 section, it lists Mark Shapiro in the Southern District of New York; the row records an October 21, 2010 sentence of 1,020 months, three years’ supervised release, and $22,075,631 restitution for conspiracy to commit securities, wire, and mail fraud, two securities-fraud counts, wire fraud, and mail fraud.

This official table gives the underlying sentence and conviction labels, but not the commutation’s replacement terms, a narrative of the fraud scheme, or a reason for clemency. The clemency record and case materials establishing those details remain missing.
